idiom_name: early-return narrow guards plus assertion functions for reusable guards
implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits the JavaScript early return and makes it pay at the type level: after a guard such as if (typeof x !== "string") throw ..., control-flow analysis narrows x to string for the rest of the scope (the handbook's Narrowing chapter), so the happy path is both flat and precisely typed. Named, reusable guards use type predicates (x is T) and assertion functions (asserts x is T), which move the check into one function while the compiler narrows at every call site; a never-typed default branch guards exhaustiveness the same way. Narrowing never crosses callbacks or async boundaries, so keep the guard in the same function as the use.
pitfalls: The non-null assertion x! skips the guard and erases the check; when the value can be absent, guard instead.
Narrowing is control-flow-local: it does not survive into callbacks, promise continuations or across an await unless the guard is repeated or the value is captured in a const.

A named guard only narrows through its declared type: an assertion signature (asserts condition / asserts x is T) keeps the call site flat, while a helper typed as returning a bare boolean narrows nothing unless it is written as a type predicate (x is T).
